wrong: Laws apply to Filipinos wherever they are
That is the personal, or nationality, principle.

That is the protective principle.

keep: The correct answer is already the shortest option, and the wrong ones are real legal maxims of similar form.

wrong: Acting by accident
An accident has no criminal intent.
Acting through carelessness
Carelessness is culpa (negligence), not intent.
Acting to defend oneself
Self-defense is a justifying circumstance, not criminal intent.
Act punishable by a special law
That is an offense.
Act punishable by a city ordinance
That is an infraction of an ordinance.
Wrong that only gives rise to damages
That is a civil wrong.
Act punishable by the RPC
That is a felony.
Act punishable by a local ordinance
That is an infraction.
Breach of a contract
A breach of contract is a civil matter.
Always unfavorable to the accused
Repeal generally benefits the accused, not the reverse.
Has no effect on pending cases
Repeal generally benefits the accused, even in pending cases.
Increases the penalty
A repeal does not increase penalties.

keep: The options are law numbers of similar form, and the correct one is tied for the longest.

wrong: Custom and religious teachings
There are no common-law crimes in the Philippines; crimes come only from written law.
Court decisions of foreign countries
Foreign decisions may persuade but are not sources of Philippine criminal law.
Police circulars and memoranda
Police issuances cannot define crimes or penalties.
Doubt resolved in favor of the prosecution
Pro reo means the reverse: doubt favors the accused.
Doubt resolved by a vote of the judges
Pro reo is a rule of interpretation, not a vote.
Doubt sends the case back for a new trial
Doubt does not mean a new trial; it is resolved in favor of the accused.
RPC applies anywhere in the world
The RPC applies mainly within Philippine territory, with limited exceptions.
RPC applies only to Filipino citizens
The RPC applies to anyone within the territory, citizen or not.
Foreign courts try local crimes
Crimes in the Philippines are tried by Philippine courts.
Killing of a child less than three days old
That is infanticide.
Killing of a stranger
That is homicide or murder, not parricide.
Killing during a robbery
That is robbery with homicide.
Robbery involves property worth more money
The value does not separate theft from robbery.
Robbery is committed only during nighttime hours
Robbery can happen at any time of day.
Robbery involves only vehicles and buildings
Robbery can involve any personal property.
Taking property quietly
That is theft, which involves no deceit.
Taking by force
That is robbery.
Misuse of public funds
That is malversation.
Threatening to kill a person in writing
That is grave threats.
Gathering of armed persons to commit rebellion
That is illegal assembly.
Publishing false news that may endanger public order
That is unlawful use of means of publication (Art. 154).
Possessing a licensed firearm at home
A licensed firearm kept at home is lawful.
Carrying a licensed firearm with a PTCFOR
Carrying a licensed firearm with a permit is lawful.
Selling firearms through a licensed dealer
Sales through a licensed dealer are lawful.
Damage to property
That is damage to property, not physical injury.
Harm to a person's reputation
That is defamation.
Taking of property
That is theft or robbery.
Persuading someone peacefully
Peaceful persuasion is not coercion.
Making a written request
A request is not coercion.
Serving a legal order
Serving a lawful order is not a crime.
Entering a home with a search warrant
Entry with a valid warrant is lawful.
Entering a home as an invited guest
An invited guest enters with consent.
Entering a public store during business hours
Trespass does not apply to public places while they are open.
Killing of a stranger
That is homicide or murder, not parricide.
Killing during a robbery
That is robbery with homicide.
Killing of any person by accident
An accidental killing may be reckless imprudence, not parricide.
Taking property secretly without force
Without violence or intimidation, it is theft.
Taking property through deceit or abuse of confidence
That is estafa.
Borrowing property without permission
Borrowing without permission is not robbery, which needs violence or intimidation.
Taking property with violence against the owner
That is robbery.
Taking property through deceit that causes damage
That is estafa.
Borrowing property with the owner's full permission
Borrowing with permission is not a crime.

wrong: To determine guilt
Guilt is decided at trial, not at preliminary investigation.
To impose the sentence
The sentence is imposed by the court after trial.
To carry out the final judgment
Execution of judgment comes after the case is decided.
Hearing where both sides present evidence
That is the trial proper.
Imposition of the penalty after conviction
That is sentencing.
Review of the decision by a higher court
That is an appeal.
Fine imposed by the court on the convicted accused
A fine is a penalty; bail is security for provisional release.
Condition attached to a parole granted by the Board
Parole conditions apply after prison; bail applies before final judgment.
Payment made to the victim to settle the case
That is a settlement, not bail.
Order to appear in court
That is a subpoena.
Order to search a place
That is a search warrant.
Order committing a convict to prison
That is a commitment order.
Arrested days after the crime
That is a later arrest, not in flagrante delicto.
Stopped before the crime begins
In flagrante means caught in the act, not before it.
Seen planning a crime
Planning alone is not being caught in the act.
Court order to arrest a person for an offense
That is a warrant of arrest.
Court order to search a place and seize items
That is a search warrant.
Money posted for the temporary release of an accused
That is bail, not a subpoena.
Place where the crime happened
That relates to venue, not jurisdiction.
Identity of the accused
Identity is a matter of proof, not jurisdiction.
Kind of punishment imposed
The penalty helps decide which court has jurisdiction, but it is not jurisdiction itself.
Date of the trial
That is the trial schedule, not venue.
Judge assigned
The assigned judge is not the venue.
Prosecutor on the case
The prosecutor is not the venue.
Right to remain silent when questioned
That is the right to remain silent.
Right to be released on bail
That is the right to bail.
Right to appeal a conviction
That is the right to appeal.
Cannot be forced to testify against oneself
That is the right against self-incrimination.
Cannot be held without charges
That is protection against arbitrary detention.
Cannot be denied a lawyer
That is the right to counsel.
Any court the accuser chooses
Venue is fixed by law, not chosen by the accuser.
Court nearest the police
Venue is where the crime was committed, not near the police.
Home town of the accused
Venue does not follow where the accused lives.
Sworn complaint filed by the victim
That is a complaint.
Report written by the arresting officer
A police report is not an information.
Written statement of an eyewitness
That is a witness affidavit.
Court decision on the case
That is a judgment.
Charge filed by the prosecutor
That is an information.
Request to review a judgment on appeal
That is an appeal.
Entitled to a lower penalty by one degree
Insanity does not merely lower the penalty; it exempts from criminal liability.
Fully liable like any other offender
Article 12 exempts insane and imbecile persons from criminal liability.
Justified, so no civil liability
Insanity exempts rather than justifies, and civil liability remains.
